Q: How to "un-ignore" files in CVS? A:

I did some experiments. First document the context:

$ ls -AGg
total 4
drwxrwxr-x 2 4096 Aug 17 11:18 CVS
$ cvs --version

Concurrent Versions System (CVS) 1.12.13-MirDebian-30 (client/server)
[...]

Note: the same version of CVS runs on my server. Now create a few test files:

$ date > test1.txt
$ date > ,test2.txt
$ ls -AGg
total 12
drwxrwxr-x 2 4096 Aug 17 11:18 CVS
-rw-rw-r-- 1   25 Aug 17 12:29 test1.txt
-rw-rw-r-- 1   25 Aug 17 12:29 ,test2.txt

And lets see what cvs thinks of these:

$ cvs -nq up
? test1.txt
$ cvs -nq up -I!
? ,test2.txt
? test1.txt

So far as expected. But if we try to use this exclamation mark in a .cvsignore file:

$ echo "!" > .cvsignore
$ cat .cvsignore 
!
$ cvs -nq up
? .cvsignore
? test1.txt
$ cvs -nq up -I!
? ,test2.txt
? .cvsignore
? test1.txt

Q: Scan directories and copy those that have more than n files A:

find is quite convenient for this kind of things. We can use it to find all album directories in the music directory, that is, directories (-type d), at a minimum depth of 2 (-mindepth 2) from current directory (find .). We can also tell find to execute a small bash script (-exec bash -c 'SCRIPT' ARGS \;) on each found directory, to test the number of files and copy them to destination if it is greater than a threshold. In the following we copy only if there are 7 files or more, and the destination directory is /tmp/sdcard. Adapt to your needs:

cd music   # must run find from there because of `mindepth 2`
find . -mindepth 2 -type d -exec bash -c 'a=("$1"/*); d="/tmp/sdcard/$1"; ((${#a[@]} >= 7)) && { mkdir -p "$d"; cp "${a[@]}" "$d"; }' _ {} \;

The bash script takes 1 parameter: the album directory, $1 inside the script, passed by find with the {} special placeholder. The _ before {} is argument number 0 of the script, that we do not use, but that is traditionally used for the script's name (and _ is my favorite for don't care). The final \; is the delimiter that find recognizes as the end of the exec command.

Note: different from other solutions (including the accepted one) this works even if the names of some of your files contain spaces, newlines or other special characters.

Note: if some of your music files are hidden (.the_hidden_song.mp3) we must enable the dotglob option to catch them with the "$1"/* pathname expansion. And if some of the album directories can be empty enabling the nullglob option is preferable. As it becomes a bit too long for a one-liner, let's define and export a bash function to encapsulate all this:

countAndCopy() {
  shopt -s dotglob nullglob   # enable dotglob and nullglob options
  a=("$1"/*)                  # populate array a with songs
  d="/tmp/sdcard/$1"          # destination directory
  if ((${#a[@]} >= 7)); then  # if more than 7 songs
    mkdir -p "$d"             # create destination directory
    cp "${a[@]}" "$d"         # copy songs
  fi
}
export -f countAndCopy        # export function such that `find` sees it
# find album directories, call function countAndCopy on each
find . -mindepth 2 -type d -exec bash -c 'countAndCopy "$1"' _ {} \;

Q: how to build compile_commands.json for arm project A:

Adding an answer incase it would be of help to someone.

Probably you are running 32-bit armcc compiler on a 64-bit PC and hence bear is a 64 bit installation. Since the compiler is a 32 bit application, a in-built 32 bit library of bear installation is searched for loading which will not be present in your installation.

The official documentation has mentioned this problem here.

Many vendor cross-toolchains still ship a 32-bit compiler driver binary even on a 64-bit host (common for older embedded SDKs distributed as prebuilt binaries); loading a 64-bit preload library into that 32-bit process fails with a “wrong ELF class” error from the dynamic linker. The build still completes, but that invocation is not intercepted, so its source file is silently missing from compile_commands.json

Q: Autonomous mode / wrapper for Claude Code? A:

The stops you are seieng come from two different mechanisms, and they have different fixes. Neither fix is a wrapper, and no wrapper can safely guarantee an indefinite unattended run.

On permission prompts, current Claude Code has an auto permission mode in which the session acts without asking, but it is a research preview with version, plan, provider, and model requirements. Where you cannot use it, acceptEdits plus narrowly scoped allow rules for the commands your task actually needs (or dontAsk) removes most propmts. bypassPermissions removes a real safety boundary, so confine it to an isolated wokrtree or container that can tolerate every side effect the session is permitted to cause. The command-line form of that same mode is --dangerously-skip-permissions (claude --dangerously-skip-permissions), so the isolation caveat covers it too.

On the "should I continue?" check-ins: these are the model hedging on an underspecified goal, and the fix is in the prompt, not in tooling. State the acceptance criteria and the the exact test commands; which files and systems are in scope; which operations still require aprpoval; when to retry, when to change approach, and when to stop; and what evidence and summary to leave if blocked. Decisions you would answer anyway, answer up front. Given a testable definition of done, the test-reflect-iterate loop you want is what fills the time between check-ins.

A loop or orchestrator that re-prompts the CLI until a task list is empty (the approach in the other answers) does help with run length: when the session stops, the wrapper starts it again. What it cannot do is remove the reasons the session stops. Authentication, rate limits, missing requirements, failing tests, genuine ambiguity, and exhausted context still need you, and a looped session making unspecified product decisions unsupervised is a risk, not autonomy. Use notification hooks so a wait for input or permission pings you instead of sitting in an unwatched terminal.

On supervision, as opposed to autonomy, there is a tool ClaudeIDE pen-code.com which addresses the supervision half: it launches and resumes Claude Code sessions from reusable prompt templates with model and reasoning effort set up front, tracks the work on a per-project task board, and raises attention alerts the moment a session asks a a question, wants a plan approved, or errors, so intervention happens when needed rahter than by polling. It does not address the autonomy half: it cannot make Claude Code run indefinitely or override its permission model.

Q: RPi3B+ AArch64 kernel in `ttbr1` region: instruction fetch succeeds after `br` to `ttbr1` region, but first data access causes Data Abort (EC=0x25) A:

This answer is only for other users which run into the same issue on real hardware. I'm currently working on the project too and fixed the issue. Enabling caches in startup fixed the issue.

The problem wasn't TLB related as the OP guessed. It was because in the kernel the locking mechanism (Spinloop and Mutex) where implemented with atomic reads and writes from Rust. These atomic reads and writes are assembled to the AArch64 exclusive load (ldaxr, ldxr, ...) and store (stxr, ...) instructions. On real hardware these instructions need enabled instruction and data cache. If not these instructions don't work correctly.

EDIT:

Unfortunately I can't explain the reason why the exclusive load and store instructions don't work properly on real hardware when the caches are disabled. They caused a dead lock. I have asked this in the official ARM support community forum. But hope maybe somebody of the SO users can explain it too.

Q: Elementor form custom webhook returns "error" message A:

The form submission itself is working because the submitted data is successfully appearing under Elementor → Submissions. However, after submitting the form:

  • The submit button keeps loading/spinning.

  • The success message is not displayed.

  • The email notification is not sent.

  • The form does not complete the submission successfully from the frontend.

I have also configured SMTP because I want the form notification emails to be sent through SMTP.

I checked my WordPress debug.log and found this error:

PHP Fatal error: Uncaught Error: Call to undefined function PHPMailer\PHPMailerenter image description hereMy question is:

Why is Elementor saving the form submission successfully but not showing the success message or sending the email? Is the PHPMailer\PHPMailer\mail() error causing this issue, and how can I correctly fix the email/SMTP configuration so that the Elementor form completes successfully and sends the notification email?

I would appreciate any guidance on what I should check in WordPress, PHP, Elementor, or the SMTP configuration.
